title: The creation of Israel, the 1948 war and the Nakba
summary: On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted to partition British-ruled Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under international administration; Jewish leaders accepted the plan, Palestinian Arab and wider Arab leaders rejected it, and civil war broke out. On 14 May 1948, as the British Mandate ended, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, and the next morning Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraqi forces invaded; when the 1949 armistice agreements ended the war, Israel held about 78 percent of Mandatory Palestine, Transjordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt held the Gaza Strip. During the fighting an estimated 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinian Arabs, about half the Arab population of Palestine, fled or were expelled from their homes and hundreds of Arab towns and villages were depopulated, events Palestinians call the Nakba (Arabic for "catastrophe").
why: Israelis remember the war as their War of Independence, which secured the Jewish state that the Zionist movement had sought since the late 19th century; Palestinians mark the Nakba each year on 15 May, and the fate of the refugees, whose return or compensation the UN General Assembly called for in December 1948, remains a key issue in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.
also: Israel lost 6,373 people, about 1 percent of its population; Arab deaths are uncertain, with estimates in the thousands. In the three years after the war a similar number of Jews migrated, fled or were expelled from Arab states, about 260,000 of whom went to Israel.

title: The Iranian Revolution
summary: Protests against Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose rule many Iranians saw as corrupt, repressive and too dependent on the United States, began in January 1978 after a government-planted newspaper article attacked the exiled cleric Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, and grew into a broad uprising of clerics, liberal nationalists and leftists whose strikes and mass demonstrations paralysed the country. The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, Khomeini returned on 1 February to a welcome by several million people, and on 11 February the army declared itself neutral and the monarchy fell. After a referendum in March 1979 Iran became an Islamic Republic, and a new constitution approved in December 1979 made Khomeini its Supreme Leader.
why: The revolution replaced a pro-Western monarchy with a theocratic republic built on Khomeini's doctrine of guardianship of the Islamic jurist (velayat-e faqih), and the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran on 4 November 1979, when 52 Americans were held hostage for 444 days, caused a lasting rupture between Iran and the United States.
also: The death toll is disputed: the Islamic Republic cites 60,000 "martyrs", but historians' estimates for January 1978 to February 1979 are far lower, from about 500 to 3,000.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Casualties of the Iranian Revolution

title: The genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda
summary: On 6 April 1994 a plane carrying Rwanda's president Juvénal Habyarimana and the president of Burundi was shot down as it prepared to land in Kigali (responsibility is still disputed), and within hours Hutu extremists in the army and the Presidential Guard and militias such as the Interahamwe began systematically killing Tutsi civilians and moderate Hutu, among them Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana. Over about 100 days, incited by local officials and by radio broadcasts that called Tutsi "cockroaches", militias and ordinary villagers killed their neighbours, mostly with machetes, at roadblocks, in homes and in the churches and schools where victims had sought refuge, and hundreds of thousands of women were raped. The killing ended in July when the mainly Tutsi Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) rebel army took Kigali on 4 July and the north-west by 18 July.
why: An estimated 500,000 to 800,000 people were killed, most of them Tutsi, while the outside world failed to intervene: after ten Belgian peacekeepers were murdered and countries pulled out their troops, the UN peacekeeping force was cut from 2,165 to 270. The genocide led to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, and the flight of some two million Hutu refugees into neighbouring countries, mainly Zaire, helped trigger the Congo wars.
also: Death-toll estimates differ: Human Rights Watch estimated at least half a million (about 507,000 Tutsi, roughly three-quarters of Rwanda's Tutsi population), scholarly estimates of Tutsi deaths range from about 500,000 to 662,000, and the Rwandan government's count is over one million.

sources.title: United Nations Outreach Programme on the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda: Historical background

title: The Paris Agreement on climate change
summary: On 12 December 2015, at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP21) at Le Bourget near Paris, 195 countries and the European Union adopted by consensus a treaty to hold the rise in global temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Instead of imposing targets, it asks every country to set its own plan for cutting greenhouse-gas emissions, a Nationally Determined Contribution, and to submit a stronger one every five years; the agreement was signed in New York on 22 April 2016 and entered into force on 4 November 2016.
why: Unlike the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, which set binding targets for only a limited set of countries, it brought developing countries into emissions planning as well, and almost every country has joined; but emissions kept rising, the United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026, and 2024 was the hottest year on record, more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

sources.title: United Nations Climate Action: The Paris Agreement
Wikipedia: 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference

title: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
summary: In 2014, after protests in Kyiv ousted the pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych, Russia seized and annexed Crimea and backed separatist forces in the Donbas, where fighting killed about 14,000 people before 2022. On 24 February 2022 President Vladimir Putin announced a "special military operation" and Russian forces invaded from Belarus towards Kyiv, from Crimea in the south and from the Donbas in the east; they withdrew from around Kyiv by April, revealing the Bucha massacre, and Ukrainian counteroffensives retook most of Kharkiv Oblast and the city of Kherson in late 2022. The war then became a costly war of attrition, with Russia occupying roughly a fifth of Ukraine.
why: It is the largest and deadliest war in Europe since the Second World War: estimates of military casualties (killed and wounded) on both sides range from about 1.3 million to 2 million by mid-2026, though all such figures are uncertain, and the UN had verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths, which it believes is an undercount, while 6 to 7 million Ukrainians fled abroad, Europe's largest refugee crisis since 1945.
also: On 2 March 2022 the UN General Assembly voted 141 to 5, with 35 abstentions, to demand that Russia withdraw its forces from Ukraine; many countries imposed sanctions on Russia, and the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and other Russian officials.
